headline: Peanut bunker boiling off Cuttyhunk — the albies are close, but not here yet
subhead: Stripers and blues are tearing through bait balls all week in the rips; the first false albacore of the season hasn't shown, but every signal says soon.
body_markdown:
The bait told me everything I needed to know before I even got the boat wet Tuesday morning. Peanut bunker, thick as smoke, pushed up against the rocks at the mouth of Quick's Hole, and every few seconds the surface would dimple and burst — not albies, not yet, but stripers working from underneath like they were being paid by the fish. That's the story of Buzzards Bay and the Vineyard right now: bunker everywhere, predators stacked under them, and everybody standing around asking the same question. Where are the albies?

We flagged this last week — said the August 12 new moon would be the trigger, that building tidal current through the rips would push bait hard enough to pull bonito and false albacore into range at Robinson's Hole and Menemsha. Two days past that moon, the current is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. Vineyard Sound is ripping harder on the last two hours of the ebb than it has all month, and the bait is bunched into current seams instead of spread thin across the flats. That's the setup. What's missing is the confirmation — no albie, no bonito on the deck yet in this stretch of water, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. Close doesn't count on a fish scale.

What IS happening, and happening hard, is bass. The bunker-driven blitz pattern that's been running from Narragansett Bay clear up into Buzzards has our water fully in its grip. I had fish busting on the surface off the west end of Naushon early Wednesday, right at first light, working peanut bunker against the current line where the Elizabeth Islands chain funnels water between the Bay and the Sound. Twenty-six to thirty-four inches, mostly schoolies with a scattering of slot fish mixed in, and they wanted a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chunk of white pork rind more than anything with hooks on a swimming plug. When they got fussy on the plug bite, a 1-ounce Deadly Dick cast right into the boil and swept with the current out-produced everything else in the box two to one.

Cuttyhunk has been the most consistent piece of this puzzle. The rip off Canapitsit Channel, running on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide change, has held bass and bluefish shoulder to shoulder in the froth. Bluefish are riding this bunker wave just like the bass are — snapper blues thick in Menemsha Pond and Lake Tashmoo, adult class fish four to six pounds busting bait off Gay Head on the outgoing. If you want blues specifically, small metal — a half-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins — thrown into the surface chop and retrieved fast will get bit before your bucktail even sinks. They're not subtle right now.

Robinson's Hole is where I'm spending my mornings, because that's historically where the first bonito of the year shows, and the current structure there is textbook right now — hard rip on the ebb, bait pinned against the western edge near the Naushon shoreline, and enough depth change to hold fish through the tide swing. I fished it Thursday on the last two hours of the ebb into dead low and came up with bass to 30 inches and blues, no bonito, no albies. That doesn't mean they're not close. Water's warm, bait's dense, and there's a real chance somebody on this stretch of coast puts one in the box within the next few days — Montauk, Block Island, Fishers Island Sound, and this water are all lined up as the most likely first spots. I'd rather tell you honestly that it hasn't happened here yet than sell you a fish that isn't in the boat.

Fluke has been a quieter, steadier story. Working the drift off the north side of the Vineyard between Oak Bluffs and East Chop, in 20 to 30 feet on a moving tide, has produced keeper fish to 22 inches on a white Gulp Swimming Mullet paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom on the drift. It's not the Nantucket Shoals numbers you're hearing about further east, but it's honest fishing, and it's holding up better than it did in July.

Look — if I had one morning this coming week, I'd be back at Robinson's Hole on the ebb, or working Menemsha Bight where the current funnels bait past the jetty into open water. The tidal flow is building the way it should this many days past the new moon, the bait density is there, and the warm water pushing in from the south has every ingredient stacked for that first albie flash. I'd keep a rod rigged with a small Albie Snax or a Deadly Dick ready on deck at all times, because when it happens here, it happens fast and it's usually a blitz before you've even seen the fish. Until then, the stripers and blues are giving us plenty to do, and that's a good problem to have while we wait.
